blocks.text: A glucometer is a portable device used to measure blood glucose concentration, usually from a small sample of capillary blood obtained by finger prick.
It is used in the screening and monitoring of diabetes mellitus, the detection of hypoglycaemia, and the assessment of patients with suspected glucose disturbances.
Typical OSCE instruction: “Identify the instrument, list its uses, demonstrate capillary blood glucose measurement, interpret the result, and discuss precautions and complications.”
A. Handheld glucometer
Uses a disposable test strip and a small blood sample.
Uses: Bedside glucose measurement, diabetes monitoring and assessment of suspected hypoglycaemia.
B. Hospital point-of-care glucose meter
A clinical device used by trained staff, sometimes with patient identification, quality-control and electronic documentation features.
Uses: Emergency departments, wards, operating theatres and critical care.
C. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) system
Uses a sensor inserted under the skin to estimate glucose in interstitial fluid.

Important distinction: A CGM is not a conventional finger-prick glucometer. It provides trends and repeated readings, but its measurements can differ from blood glucose, particularly during rapid changes.

blocks.text: OSCE distinction: The lancet punctures the skin; the test strip collects the blood sample; the meter measures the glucose concentration.
Most modern glucometers use an enzymatic electrochemical method. The blood sample reacts with enzymes on the test strip, producing an electrical signal related to the glucose concentration.
The meter processes this signal and displays a numerical result.
Some devices use different technologies, and not every strip uses the same enzyme system.

items.text: mmol/L — commonly used in Nigeria and many other countries.
mg/dL — commonly used in the United States and some other settings.

blocks.text: Conversion:
\[ \text{mg/dL} \approx \text{mmol/L}\times18 \]
For example, 5.0 mmol/L is approximately 90 mg/dL.

blocks.text: Important: A glucometer is useful for rapid assessment, but laboratory testing may be required to confirm a diagnosis of diabetes. In an emergency, treatment of suspected severe hypoglycaemia should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory confirmation.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. How to measure capillary blood glucose: OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: 0 of 14 steps completed
Reset
1. Perform hand hygiene, introduce yourself, confirm patient identity, explain the procedure and obtain consent.
2. Check the meter, compatible test strips, expiry dates and any required quality-control status.
3. Confirm the units displayed by the meter: mmol/L or mg/dL.
4. Put on appropriate gloves and prepare a single-use safety lancet.
5. Ask the patient to wash their hands with soap and water and dry them thoroughly, where feasible.
6. Insert the test strip according to the manufacturer's instructions and ensure the meter is ready.
7. Choose the side of a fingertip, avoiding damaged, infected or previously punctured areas where possible.
8. Use the single-use lancet to puncture the skin safely.
9. If needed, gently encourage a blood drop without excessive squeezing.
10. Apply the blood to the designated area of the strip according to the device instructions.
11. Wait for the meter to display the result and assess whether it is clinically plausible.
12. Record the result, units, time, relevant symptoms and relation to meals or treatment.
13. Dispose of the lancet immediately into an approved sharps container and discard the strip appropriately.
14. Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene and act on abnormal results according to the clinical situation.
**Why use the side of the fingertip?**
The sides of the fingertip are generally less painful than the centre while providing a suitable capillary blood sample.
For routine adult testing, the middle or ring finger is often convenient. In infants and young children, use only an age-appropriate approved sampling method and device.
**Why must the hands be clean and dry?**

Food residue, particularly sugar-containing substances, can falsely elevate the result. Excess water can dilute the sample, while alcohol or other cleaning agents that have not dried properly may interfere with measurement.
Best practice: Soap and water followed by thorough drying is preferred when possible.
These are general reference points for non-pregnant adults, not universal treatment targets.

blocks.text: For diagnosis, fasting plasma glucose and laboratory-based criteria should be used according to the applicable guideline. A bedside capillary reading alone should not ordinarily be used to establish a new diagnosis of diabetes.

blocks.text: If a conscious patient can swallow safely and has hypoglycaemia, give rapid-acting oral glucose according to the local protocol and recheck the glucose after approximately 10–15 minutes.

If the patient is unconscious, having seizures, or unable to swallow safely, do not give anything orally. Activate emergency care and administer appropriate glucose treatment according to the local protocol.

blocks.title: High glucose may be associated with:

items.text: Polyuria and polydipsia.
Dehydration.
Weight loss.
Vomiting and abdominal pain.
Deep, laboured breathing and altered consciousness in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

blocks.text: A patient with suspected DKA or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state requires urgent clinical assessment, including appropriate laboratory investigations. A glucometer alone cannot diagnose or exclude these emergencies.
There are no major absolute contraindications to routine capillary glucose testing, but appropriate precautions are essential.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the function of a glucometer?
It measures blood glucose concentration, usually using a small capillary blood sample.
Q2. Why should the patient's hands be washed and dried?
To remove contaminants that may distort the result and to avoid dilution of the blood sample.
Q3. What glucose level is commonly used as the hypoglycaemia alert threshold?
Below 3.9 mmol/L in many diabetes protocols. Below 3.0 mmol/L is clinically significant hypoglycaemia.
Q4. Can a glucometer diagnose diabetes definitively?
A bedside meter is useful for screening and monitoring, but laboratory-based diagnostic criteria are generally required to establish a new diagnosis.
Q5. Why should lancets never be reused between patients?
Reuse can transmit blood-borne infections and cause sharps injuries.
Q6. What is your immediate action if an unconscious patient has a glucose of 2.1 mmol/L?

Activate emergency assistance, assess and support airway, breathing and circulation, and give appropriate emergency glucose treatment according to the local protocol. Do not administer oral glucose to an unconscious patient.
Q7. Why might a glucometer be unreliable in a neonate?
Accuracy can be affected by low glucose concentrations, neonatal haematocrit and poor peripheral perfusion, depending on the device.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. Common mistakes that lose OSCE marks

items.text: Failing to check the units.
Using expired or incompatible test strips.
Sampling a finger contaminated with food or sugar.
Applying insufficient blood or using the strip incorrectly.
Excessively squeezing the finger.
Reusing lancets.
Failing to document the result and relevant symptoms.
Treating a critically unwell patient as stable because a glucose reading appears normal.
Giving oral glucose to a patient who cannot swallow safely.
Delaying treatment of severe hypoglycaemia while awaiting laboratory confirmation.
